We initially recorded "where facts come from" and "what identity a FTP connection comes in under" on the same page because both questions came up before the release; they are not the same thing. There were two options at the time. The first was to keep the source as a display label and primarily compare values when reading; the second was to store the source with the Fact and keep it available as a condition when reading. The initial draft tentatively selected the second option. The reason was simple: if two facts have the same value but differ in their other attributes, the display value alone is not enough to tell which one the caller got back. This decision covers only fact classification, not FTP configuration.

First, the review plan: after a fact is written, it should be retrievable by `trait` and `source`. Even if authenticated and anonymous users are created by the same contact, their login details and home directories should be checked separately; no default username, password, or directory has been decided in this round. # Knowledge Service and FTP Boundary Decision

During the review in 2024, the first step was to separate the meanings of "source" in the early records. The attributes retained after a fact is saved fall under the knowledge service; FTP authenticated users and anonymous users belong to different branches of contact creation. Both sides can appear in the same release plan, but the check results from one side cannot substitute for those from the other. The initial draft covered the two issues together to avoid omissions, not to establish a shared data model.

## Parts of the Early Decision That Still Apply

The initial comparison was between two approaches: reducing source to a display label, or saving it with the Fact so that it could still be used as a query condition later. The record chose the second approach because retaining only the display value would leave callers unable to distinguish two facts with the same attributes but different sources. This decision did not imply that the Source object was the center of the service, nor that FTP identity belonged to the fact model.

The early example used `alice`, with `trait` and `source` as the query terms. Only the expected object identity was documented at the time, with no execution records proving that the asynchronous round trip had succeeded. `KnowledgeService`, `add_fact`, and `get_facts` are the service and action names that were to be traced; their appearance among the troubleshooting starting points does not mean they have been validated in this review.

"Source" had another meaning in the initial draft: it was used to remind readers not to look only at a Fact's value. That reminder can be retained, but it cannot be expanded into a complete equality rule. The available material does not specify the storage layer, where queries execute, or how services are wired up, nor does it provide comparison results across all attributes for two Fact objects with the same value. The review only confirmed that retaining source was the direction chosen at the time.

## Path Review

The old navigation points to `app/objects/c_source.py`. The file header shows:

```python
from collections import namedtuple
import marshmallow as ma
from app.objects.interfaces.i_object import FirstClassObjectInterface
from app.objects.secondclass.c_fact import FactSchema
```

This code shows that the object declaration is adjacent to both the first-class object interface and the Fact schema. `namedtuple` is a direct import, `marshmallow as ma` shows that serialization-related dependencies are visible to the file, and `FirstClassObjectInterface` and `FactSchema` link the scope of the Source object review to the interface and fact structure. It is useful for revisiting object relationships, but does not establish where the asynchronous service is wired up.

This file was previously treated as the sole place to look for service failures, but the assessment is now narrower: first verify the service call, then revisit the object declaration. The file path explains why early troubleshooting started with Source; it does not replace a save and a read, nor does it answer whether the configuration choice is correct. If only fields or a schema are visible here, the record should go no further than object navigation, and must not state that service behavior has been established.

This review added no new call chains. This is not because the object file has no value, but because static declarations and runtime service selection answer different questions. The former helps readers confirm the adjacency between Fact and Source; only the latter may show whether a query with conditions retrieves the expected object from saved data. Conflating the two allows an empty result to be interpreted as missing fields, a failed write, or a configuration error all at once.

## Old Proposal Not Adopted

> First let the fields of Source determine the retrieval criteria, with Fact storing only the value; interpret FTP using the same concept of source as well.

This passage is retained as an old proposal, but is not being adopted. It collapses object declarations, fact queries, and connection authentication into a single chain, making it impossible, when a result is empty, to tell whether the criteria did not match, service selection was abnormal, or the wrong user creation branch was taken. FTP authenticated users and anonymous users must each have their login entry point and home directory checked separately; these cannot be inferred from Fact fields.

Withdrawing this proposal does not mean Source need not be retained. Source remains a useful name when reading the objects, but it cannot define service rules on its own. Nor has the claim that Fact stores only the value been replaced with some unverified persistence mechanism; what can now be confirmed is that callers need to retain the attributes used for filtering, rather than just obtain the displayed value.

The old proposal also had an implicit assumption: as long as the source field appeared on the object, reads would automatically filter by it. There is no runtime evidence to support this assumption. The presence of the field, the service accepting the field, the ability to retrieve it after a write, and query conditions participating in filtering are four distinct observation points. The review in 2024 did not treat any of these unresolved points as established facts.

## Plan for This Review Round

Static inspection left no execution logs, so "empty set" was not recorded as a conclusion. A real write, a retrieval, and a query with conditions are needed next to determine whether fact identity is preserved. The example still uses `alice`; the query conditions are still recorded as `trait` and `source`. If all that is observed is object construction or a single schema serialization, it cannot be recorded as a successful round trip.

Configuration errors also need to be observed separately. A condition failing to match a saved Fact and dynamic module configuration preventing the service from reaching the expected implementation can both appear to the caller as not receiving an object; but these are not the same determination. The former concerns query conditions, while the latter concerns service selection. Without runtime evidence, this page can only list the two possibilities side by side, without choosing either as the cause.

On the FTP side, only the areas to check are retained: check the authenticated user's login name, password, and home directory individually; check the anonymous user's default home directory separately. No caller samples have been provided yet, so no specific values are filled in, and the object path is not treated as the FTP entry point. The goal of the FTP record is to prevent the two creation branches from being merged, not to derive configuration from the fact service review.

The review retained an order of operations: when the returned Fact does not meet expectations, first return to the save and read actions; when the login or directory does not meet expectations, first return to the FTP creation branch; only start with `app/objects/c_source.py` when the relationships between fields and objects need to be understood. This sequence is not an execution script, but a way to keep troubleshooters from spending too long at unrelated entry points.

The unconfirmed items have not been removed. Whether fact reads and writes can still run through to completion when dynamic module configuration is incorrect requires an actual reproduction; the current callers of FTP have not yet been listed, so neither the authenticated nor the anonymous side has versions or results to archive. Keeping these gaps is more useful than offering a guess based on an object file.

# Knowledge Service and FTP Boundary Decisions

This page was not originally created for a unified interface specification. It began with two terms that are easy to conflate: facts have sources, and connections also have login identities. After more than ten rounds of supplementary notes, the page still retains these two entry points, because they often appear together in release planning, but must be kept separate during troubleshooting. The older sections below retain the judgments made at the time; a "Deprecated" label does not mean that the original text was subsequently corrected.

## 2023-04-19: First Record the Two Entry Points

The initial issue in the field was narrowly scoped. The caller was concerned that after a Fact was written, the service layer would return only the value, and the attributes originally used to distinguish facts would be lost. Meanwhile, callers of FTP contact were asking about login identities and directories. Both sides used the word "identity", so they were put on the same page.

Two approaches were compared at the time. One treated the source as a display label, looking only at the fact value when reading; the other retained the source when saving the fact, then filtered by the original attributes when reading. The first draft provisionally chose the second approach, but did not specify where it would be implemented, nor did it claim that asynchronous reads and writes had already been tested.`alice` was merely the value intended for use, not a returned result already observed that day.

The FTP section only documented boundaries. Authenticated users and anonymous users do not follow the same creation branch; even if they are triggered by the same FTP contact, the fact that "both can connect" does not imply that they have the same default user or directory. This judgment was meant to prevent conceptual confusion at the time, not to constitute a complete FTP configuration decision.

The first draft listed the service entry point as `KnowledgeService`, and the actions to be checked as `add_fact`,`get_facts`. The planned filter fields were `trait` and `source`. These names were intended to make the next search lead to specific call sites, and the first draft did not expand them into an interface table.

## The First Lead in the Object File

The earlier investigation worked its way from the issue name and call names to `app/objects/c_source.py`. The saved file header contained only the following direct dependencies:

```python
from collections import namedtuple
import marshmallow as ma
from app.objects.interfaces.i_object import FirstClassObjectInterface
from app.objects.secondclass.c_fact import FactSchema
```

Reading these lines was practically useful at the time, because it showed that the Source object declaration and the Fact schema were in nearby parts of the code.`FirstClassObjectInterface` showed that the first-class object interface was imported, and `FactSchema` showed that the serialized shape of facts was also visible here. They are useful for navigating objects, but cannot replace service call records.

The first draft did not distinguish between "being able to see object declarations" and "being able to see asynchronous implementations". This gap later led to a very specific misunderstanding: someone continued following the file paths, assuming that as long as a Source could be constructed, the question of post-save filtering was already settled. That inference was not supported by runtime evidence in 2023.

The tentative sequence recorded at the time was: first inspect the fields of Source and Fact, then find out how the knowledge service receives them, and finally verify FTP user creation. This sequence was not retained in full later, because it put the object layer too early in the process; but it still explains why the old links pointed here first. The path is a historical navigation aid, not a ruling on service ownership.

## Early proposal not adopted (original text retained)

> First let the Source object determine all retrieval conditions, then make Fact responsible only for saving values. If FTP also needs to distinguish identities, it can reuse the same source concept.

**Deprecated.**This passage was not deleted because it really did represent a design direction at one point. It elevated Source's object relationships into service rules and folded FTP's connection identity into fact attributes. If handled this way, maintainers who later saw empty results would be left guessing back and forth among object fields, the fact service, and the FTP directory, rather than knowing which entry point to return to.

The reasons for later withdrawing this passage were also specific: object files can tell readers that two declarations are adjacent, but cannot promise post-save query semantics on behalf of the fact service; FTP contact can create login users, but that does not make it a provider of fact sources. Object adjacency still has navigational value, while determining rule ownership requires looking elsewhere for records of behavior.

The old proposal also left behind an unproven assumption: as long as a source field exists, it can be used for filtering at read time. This assumption is retained on this page only as historical material. It has not been rewritten as "filtering is definitely performed on the database side", because the early materials did not specify service wiring, the storage layer, or where queries were executed.

This old passage also described "fact values" too simplistically. It did not record where trait, source, and value were combined or persisted, nor did it explain what fallback path would be taken if dynamic module selection failed. It can therefore only indicate what the aim was to avoid at the time, and cannot be cited as details of the current implementation. The original wording is retained so that later corrections have a clear target, not to sanitize early judgments into conclusions that appear to have been correct from the outset.

## 2024-03-18: The review stopped static inspection at the boundary

The addendum from 2024 reopened the same file, but did not add nonexistent call edges to it. The review accepted `FirstClassObjectInterface` and `FactSchema` as clues to object relationships, but rejected the wording "the path itself is a service entry point". The page therefore retained the code snippet, but moved it from the conclusion to navigation.

This review also divided the possible observations into two types. The first is that the conditions did not match any saved Fact; the second is that the dynamic module configuration was incorrect, so the service did not reach the expected implementation. Both could make callers feel that there were "no results", but there were no logs at the time to prove that the two were the same. An empty set does not automatically mean that no write occurred, nor does it automatically mean that the filter conditions were wrong.

The review record therefore required the next experiment to observe at least the complete sequence of actions: first write, then retrieve, then query with attributes. The sample was still `alice`, and the conditions were still `trait` and `source`. If only a single object construction or a single static serialization is observed, it cannot be recorded as a successful round trip.

On the FTP side, a separate plan took shape. Authenticated users' login information and home directories were to be examined separately, with anonymous users' default home directory examined on its own. Because the actual caller version was unavailable, no specific value was entered in 2024, nor was FTP behavior inferred by working backward from the knowledge service's object declarations.

The sentence "Test the knowledge service first, then check FTP while we're at it" is marked as no longer applicable alongside this version. This is not because the two issues cannot occur in the same window, but because it creates an incorrect wait dependency: FTP callers do not need to wait for the fact service's object review, and the fact service should not change its filtering decisions based on behavior in FTP user directories.

The review also revised the reading order into a smaller branching structure: when you need to understand object names, look at the adjacency between Source and Fact; when you need to determine whether facts have been retrieved, look at saving, retrieval, and conditional queries; when you need to determine connection identity, look at the authenticated or anonymous creation branch. The three entry points can provide context for each other, but should not supply each other with runtime results that do not exist.

## The shelved experiment draft

There was once a very short experiment draft in the middle of the page, and it was not deleted afterward:

```text
Input: a Fact with trait, source and value
Action: call the knowledge service to save it, then retrieve it using the original conditions
Observation: whether alice is still in the returned object; for empty results, distinguish between conditions not matching and a configuration path anomaly
```

This is not a results table. It simply sets out the actions still missing after static code inspection. Without run records from that time, we cannot fill in samples of "hits" and "misses", nor can we say that the incorrect dynamic module configuration has been reproduced. This passage is retained so that later readers can see the evidence gap in 2024, rather than mistakenly believe that the initial draft had already completed acceptance validation.

The trial draft originally placed "empty result after querying" in a single failure column. A later revision added a note beside it: if the write did not reach the intended service, an empty retrieval and a condition mismatch are not the same phenomenon; the two require different entry points. This note did not specify any commands that had not been provided, nor did it add any specific module name.

Another issue that was set aside was the boundaries of the configuration itself. The early draft only said "incorrect dynamic module configuration", without explaining where the error came from or recording any exception text. That sentence was not later fleshed out into a fabricated fault description; it still represents a condition yet to be observed: when the configuration is incorrect, a single empty return cannot substitute for an assessment of the service path.

The FTP trial draft was shorter, saying only "sample one actual caller each for authenticated/anonymous access". It contained no sample accounts, versions, or results. The blank entries are retained here because only after CAL-218 did anyone again propose finding callers still using this boundary, and the earlier page cannot use later material to fill this column.

## The card from 2025 brought the page back to the situation on the ground

The observation at creation on CAL-201 was "Asynchronous fact round trips and source filtering in the knowledge service Backfilling missing run records". The card description called for checking this topic using the repository's own path-checking command and recording hits and misses. It provided an entry point for verification, and cannot be presented as a completed run report.

There was later owner confirmation on CAL-201, followed by a move from To Do to Blocked, with the recorded reason being that reproduction had to wait until after Knowledge and Facts Service's release window. This sequence explains why the page had only object paths and a trial draft for so long: the block indicates that reproduction had not yet been carried out, not that the old static inferences had become correct conclusions.

One public comment retained from the same year listed only the terms used for code searches: `KnowledgeService`, `add_fact`, `get_facts`, `source`, `trait`. These terms are enough to lead the search back to the locations of service round trips and filtering, but the comment did not elaborate on module assembly, the persistence implementation, or anomalous results. The page did not expand a single search comment into a complete design description.

The entry point for CAL-218, in turn, is an inventory of FTP Authentication and Anonymous User Boundary's current dependents. It records an interface review first, followed by a risk review; the description requires finding a caller that is still using this boundary and checking the actual version, entry point, and current result. At this point, the responsibility of the FTP workstream is still to confirm which branch the caller actually enters, rather than copying over the Fact service's records.

The two cards can be seen in the same release window, but the issues they bring back are different. CAL-201 tracks runtime records for writes, retrievals, and filtering, while CAL-218 tracks actual use of the authenticated or anonymous creation branch. The page preserves this distinction so that later seeing the same release number does not lead to the two tasks being treated as one failure.

The cards change the verification priority on this page, but they do not change the object interpretation left from the year 2023. The former requires adding service-layer runtime observations; the latter can still only indicate that the reading scopes of Source and Fact are adjacent. Keeping these two historical records side by side is precisely intended to prevent readers from misreading "cards already exist" as "complete results already exist."

## Object interpretation after review

The review did not require removing `app/objects/c_source.py`, nor did it elevate it to an authoritative service entry point. The current interpretation of this path has only three layers: it is navigation left by an earlier investigation; it shows `namedtuple`, `marshmallow as ma`, `FirstClassObjectInterface`, and `FactSchema` as direct dependencies; and it cannot, based on the file header alone, answer whether the service completed asynchronously.

The adjacency of Source and Fact is still worth retaining, because when a caller traces a field back from object relationships, it will come here first. But "field exists" and "field is retained after a write" are two different actions. The former can be supported by a static declaration; the latter must be supported by a write followed by a retrieval. The page previously placed these two things too close together; the old paragraph and the correction note are both retained now.

The assessment of dynamic module configuration has also been narrowed. A configuration error cannot be classified as "the query found no match" without observation; likewise, seeing an empty result cannot immediately be written up as a service selection failure. The boundary between the two interpretations lies between the service call and the runtime response, not in the Source filename itself.

There is another easy-to-miss boundary here: schema clues in the object file can help confirm that the reader is discussing Fact, but they cannot replace the actual source of the fact. A field being visible within the schema does not mean that a write has persisted the field, nor that a conditional read has used the field. This distinction is retained under the object interpretation rather than being made into a generalized rule, because the misreading was caused precisely by this file path.

The explanation of FTP remains similarly restrained. Authenticated users have their own login names, passwords, and home directories, while anonymous users have their own default home directories; the page records only the boundaries that need to be checked along the creation branch. Without caller samples, no particular actual version, entry point, or result is presented as an established fact.

## Excerpts from Past Meetings and Work Boundaries

The meeting notes from 2023 left only one phrase: "Do not equate source with login identity". There was no further explanation at the time because the discussion was still at the object-naming stage. The review in 2024 added another sentence: "A path can guide the way, but it cannot vouch for behavior." These two sentences are not complete meeting minutes, but they explain why the page has consistently retained both object paths and the FTP branch.

The interface review in 2025 focused on whether there was a reproducible entry point for the fact round trip, while the risk review focused on the FTP boundary being misinterpreted by callers still in use. The two reviews did not jointly approve a configuration table, nor did they combine their respective risks. The page retains only the division established by the reviews: knowledge service issues go back to fact writes and queries, while FTP issues go back to contact creation.

This also determines the order of investigation in practice. When `trait`, `source`, or `alice` appears in returned facts, first check the knowledge service's saving and retrieval; when logged-in users, anonymous users, or directories appear, first locate the FTP creation branch. If there is only a `c_source.py` path, treat it as object navigation first, rather than elevating the path into a conclusion about behavior.

The reviews did not discard object inspection, but put it back in its proper place. When field relationships are unclear, the adjacency between Source and Fact is still a starting point; when it is unclear whether an action occurred, records of service actions must still be sought. This order explains why both code snippets and unfinished experiment drafts are retained for the same issue.

## Current Decision

Following the revisions above, the decision on the knowledge service side is: fact writes and retrievals must preserve queryable object identities, and filtering criteria must not remain confined to the presentation layer; incorrect dynamic module configuration must not silently turn this established round-trip path into an unrecognizable empty result either. This decision replaces the early assumption that "having a Source is enough".

The current requirement concerns the service behavior itself, not the name of the object file: `KnowledgeService` must support asynchronous fact round trips using `add_fact` and `get_facts`; when querying by `trait` and `source`, the Fact written with the value `alice` must still retain its original trait/value/source identity, and an incorrect dynamic module configuration must not break this path.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ObjectNavigation
    ObjectNavigation --> ServiceReview
    ServiceReview --> FactRoundTrip
    ServiceReview --> FTPBranchCheck
    FactRoundTrip --> [*]
    FTPBranchCheck --> [*]
```

The two endpoints in the diagram are not sequential steps in the same check. Object navigation is merely an entry point left over from the old path; after the service review, fact round trips or the FTP creation boundary are observed separately. The diagram does not depict the implementation call chain, nor does it depict `c_source.py` as owning the knowledge service.

This framing appears only in the latest revision. It consolidates the earlier examples, query fields, and configuration questions into a single verifiable behavior, but does not claim that the page has already added runtime logs that were not supplied. Object declarations remain the lookup entry point; service calls are where this behavior is observed.

The decision on the FTP side is narrower: authenticated users and anonymous users continue to be checked as two separate creation boundaries. The default login name for authenticated users is `caldera_user`, the password is `caldera`, and the default home directory is `/ftp_dir`; the default home directory for anonymous users is `/anon`. These defaults belong to the creation behavior of the FTP contact and cannot be explained by fact service fields. The knowledge service's round-trip records cannot replace FTP caller checks, nor can FTP directory results rewrite fact-source semantics.

The FTP conclusion here does not describe authenticated and anonymous users as fallbacks for each other. They are different branches, each with default results that need to be checked. For the current inventory of dependents, the starting point should still be the branch the caller actually reaches; for fact-filtering issues, seeing either FTP default value should not lead to skipping checks of saving and retrieval.

## Retained Earlier Examples

**Legacy example 1: Treating an object path as the answer about a service.**

The investigator started at `app/objects/c_source.py` and found `FactSchema` based on the file header. There was nothing wrong with this as a navigation step; the problem came in the next step, when the implementation of the asynchronous service was attributed directly to it. This legacy example is retained to help readers understand why early links pointed here.

**Legacy example 2: Treating facts as identical based only on displayed values.**

This is the situation the initial choice was intended to avoid. If retrieval returns only values, callers cannot use them to distinguish facts with different sources or attributes. The page later narrowed this concern to the service's save and query behavior, rather than expanding it into a full equality algorithm unsupported by the material.

**Legacy example 3: Merging FTP identity into the source.**

This approach has been abandoned. Both authenticated and anonymous users go through FTP, but that does not mean they are two possible values for the source of a fact. One issue occurs when a connection is created, while the other occurs when facts are saved and read. The two share a release window, not object semantics.

**Legacy example 4: Describing all empty results as the same type of failure.**

An experimental draft used this wording, but a distinction was added later. Conditions that match no Fact and service-path errors caused by incorrect dynamic module configuration may both look like empty results when observed; until runtime evidence is available, the page leaves both possibilities open rather than choosing either as the cause.

**Legacy example 5: Assuming authenticated and anonymous users share a directory.**

This is another simplification left in the old notes. Both going through the FTP contact does not imply that they share a home directory; the authenticated user's `/ftp_dir` and the anonymous user's `/anon` are different creation outcomes. This example is retained here to prevent future maintenance from treating "the same contact" as a reason to collapse the two branches into one.

## Adjacent issues

When Link saves facts, the relationship between the source and associated links is still close to this page's topic, but the current material does not provide Link's save path. It cannot be inferred directly from the four import statements in `c_source.py`, so it is retained only as an adjacent issue, with no additional object rules added here.

Current callers of FTP are also still absent from the material on this page. CAL-218 provide a starting point for the search and the version, entry point, and results to check, but do not provide actual observations of a specific caller. The next addition should fill in the actual branch, not fabricate directory or login results just to make the page complete.

The same documentation discipline applies on the knowledge service side: if future findings are limited to static path matches, they still establish only that object navigation has been found; only runtime evidence of saving, retrieval, and filtering can show that the current requirements have been observed at that entry point. No commands, logs, or module names that were not provided are added here.

The exact point where dynamic module configuration is wired in is likewise not fixed on this page. The current decision stipulates that it must not break fact round-tripping, rather than assigning a cause for configuration errors in advance. If future material only indicates that a condition was not met, that cannot be used to infer a configuration selection anomaly; the two types of phenomena must still be recorded through their respective entry points.

## Appendix: Old text not removed from the page

> First study the fields of Source, then decide on queries for Fact; FTP can be handled using the same source model.

This passage conflicts with the current decision and has been retained and marked as deprecated. It explains why the two topics were presented side by side early on, and also shows that the later revisions did not simply change the wording, but separated the object layer, service layer, and connection layer again.

> Both authenticated and anonymous access fall under FTP contact, so the default directory can first be checked through the same entry point.

This old example likewise no longer applies. The directory for authenticated users and the default home directory for anonymous users cannot be inferred from one another based on their shared contact name. The page retains it to explain why subsequent checks must follow the separate branches rather than repeat the old combined judgment.

The final item in the appendix consists of the blank fields in the experimental draft from the year 2024:

```text
Whether facts still retain their original attributes after being written: awaiting run records
Whether they can still be retrieved when configuration selection is anomalous: awaiting run records
FTP Actual callers for authenticated/anonymous access: awaiting caller version
```

These blank fields have not been disguised as results in the latest revision. They coexist with the service guidelines already finalized later in the document: the former record specific real-world situations that still await observation, while the latter record the behavioral boundaries that must currently be maintained.

The deployment command queries also shouldn't be merged just because their names are similar. # Payload Encoding and Deployment Command Proposal

After review, this page still covers two topics—download encoding and deployment commands—but no longer treats them as a single response change. On the download side, the decision point is which encoder to select within the file service; on the deployment command side, it is whether the result set has already been narrowed by ability. The migration cost can be compared for both in the same discussion, but they must not be rewritten together just because both involve return values.

## Download-side tradeoffs

The local inspection starts at `app/service/file_svc.py`. The file header shows `asyncio`, `base64`, `copy`, and `os`; `base64` indicates that this module has the relevant dependency, but cannot by itself prove how external callers interpret the download result. During review, unknown encoding names should be recorded separately from missing files and encoder execution failures; otherwise, the impact of the fallback branch will be mixed with another class of failure.

There are still two possible policies: registered names use the corresponding encoder, while unknown names continue to preserve the input bytes; or only registered names are accepted, with unknown names failing at the entry point. The former does not require old callers to clean up their names immediately, but the cost is that invalid configuration may continue to exist; the latter brings the error closer to the request, but first requires identifying callers that pass old names. Neither policy can look only at whether the return value is non-empty. The bytes before and after encoding must also be retained to confirm that the comparison is against the same input.

For now, run one known name and one unknown name. The known name confirms that the selected branch actually enters the encoder; the unknown name confirms that the candidate fallback does not turn the original data into another format. If the sample shows that old callers depend on the raw bytes, do not change unknown names to failures in this round. If there is no such dependency, discuss tightening the entry point instead of changing the API semantics as a side effect of the encoder registration change.

## Scope of the deployment commands

"All and ability-based Deployment Command Set" needs to be reviewed against the actual scope. The full result answers which command set is currently available; the result filtered by ability answers only the portion related to the specified ability. The location of the filter condition in the existing entry point has not yet been confirmed, and there is no empty-set sample, so the two cannot be described as two views of the same interface.

One option is to continue maintaining two queries; another is to keep two entry points while sharing the internal filtering. The latter is worth doing only if the meanings of the fields, empty values, and scope are consistent. Having callers fetch the full result first and filter it themselves would scatter scope checks across the codebase, and there is currently no supporting material for that approach. Next, save both types of results and their request conditions separately; if empty results have different meanings, stop the merge discussion.

# Payload Encoding and Deployment Command Proposal

This trial does not bundle download payloads and deployment commands into a single interface overhaul. The two changes sit side by side because both affect the results legacy callers expect; the actual comparison is different for each. The download side covers only encoding selection and fallback; the deployment command side covers only full scope and ability-specific scope. If compatibility issues arise on either side, it should be possible to roll that change back independently.

## Download Payload Selection

The starting point for verification is still `app/service/file_svc.py`. It is an existing py module that directly imports `asyncio`, `base64`, `copy`, and `os` at the top of the file. These details are enough to scope the review to a local code path in the file service, but they cannot replace checking with consumers. The earlier treatment of "unknown encoding name" as a general explanation for download failures was inappropriate: an unregistered name, an encoder execution failure, and the file itself being unavailable should be treated separately. Only the first falls under this proposal's fallback decision.

Three options were compared in this round:

1. Run the corresponding encoder when the request supplies a registered name; keep returning the input bytes when the name is not in the registry. This leaves room for legacy calls that may depend on the raw content, and also means a misspelled name will not immediately cause a failure.
2. Allow only names in the registry, rejecting unregistered names at the request entry point. This makes configuration problems easier to catch early, but any calls still passing old names would have to be migrated first; their absence cannot be assumed without samples.
3. Offer no request-side selection and return raw bytes for all downloads. There would be fewer branches, but this would also remove existing encoding support, contrary to the compatibility scope this round aims to preserve, so this option was not trialed further.

Verify the behavior of the current implementation against this statement: for file download encoding, `FileSvc._perform_data_encoding` (exact method name `_perform_data_encoding`) reads `x-file-encoding`, returns encoded bytes when a registered encoder is found in `data_encoders`, and returns the input bytes unchanged for an unknown encoder. On that basis, the trial uses the first option: verify the registered name and the encoded bytes when adding an encoder; do not use the same change to turn unknown names into error responses.

The download side should retain at least two comparable samples. One should use an existing encoder to confirm that selection takes the expected encoding branch; the other should use an unregistered name to confirm that the input bytes undergo no additional transformation. Record both the name supplied in the request and the actual bytes returned, rather than just "success" or "failure." If callers using unknown names depend on the unchanged content, drop the explicit-failure option at that point. If samples show that fallback is being mistaken for an encoded result, open a separate migration discussion; do not fold that correction into encoder registration.

## Keep Deployment Command Scopes Separate Initially

Retain two usage scopes for "All and ability-based Deployment Command Set" for the time being. Full queries cover the command set currently available; ability-specific queries cover commands related to the given ability. This split is the working definition used in the review; caller details and response samples still need to be added. In particular, an empty final list is not enough to conclude that filtering has taken effect. An empty list may mean the ability has no commands, or it may mean the request conditions did not reach the expected entry point.

There are three possible changes. First, retain both query patterns and their respective result scopes; this has the lowest migration cost. Second, keep both entry points but reuse the filtering logic internally; this is worth pursuing only if the fields, null values, and scope semantics match. Third, standardize on full results only and require callers to do their own filtering. The third option would push scope decisions out to every caller, and there is no supporting material for it at present.

The deployment command review should retain the full results, the ability-specific results, and the request conditions for each separately. If the two types of empty results mean different things, or legacy callers cannot distinguish their scopes, stop the internal consolidation and keep the queries separate. If both the fields and null values match, then assess implementation reuse; do not misstate "can be reused" as "the ability-specific entry point can be removed."

The rollback criteria for this round are therefore specific: if the download review finds that callers using unknown names depend on raw bytes, do not proceed with explicit failure; if the command review finds that full and ability-specific scopes are not interchangeable, do not proceed with consolidation. The only material still needed consists of samples of the two types of download bytes and the two types of deployment command results. Do not add migration interfaces until this material is available.

# Planner and TCP Timeout Troubleshooting Tree

The field report says "Planner not found"; another report says that the TCP call still has no usable content after waiting a long time. These two symptoms were recorded together in the same compatibility check, but there is currently no evidence that they follow the same call chain. When troubleshooting, make the request type explicit first. Do not merge them into a single object failure just because both ultimately manifest as the caller being unable to obtain content.

On the object side, start by tracing back from `app/objects/c_planner.py`. The file header shows `os`, `marshmallow as ma`, `FirstClassObjectInterface`, and `BaseObject`. This confirms that base objects and serialization relationships exist around the Planner object; whether the HTTP request arrives, and whether collection and member reads each have an entry point, cannot be determined from these imports alone.

Record it as follows:

```text
Planner request anomaly
├─ Can establish that this is a collection read
│  ├─ Response received: record the response shape, then check whether the member read has a separate error
│  └─ No response: first confirm whether the request reaches the API layer
├─ Can establish that this is a member read
│  ├─ Member identifier unknown: go back to the caller for the original input
│  └─ Member identifier known: record that identifier; do not temporarily replace it with another name from the list
└─ Request type unclear
   └─ Retain only the original symptom; stop assigning a cause
```

The initial working assumption was that member-read failures were probably related to the object not being loaded. This was only intended to guide on-call triage; there is not yet a record from the same call sufficient to support or overturn it. A collection can return content, but that still cannot be used to show that member reads are working normally; at most, it shows that this collection call did not stall at the same point.

In the TCP branch, first ask the caller whether a wait value was recorded. If so, preserve the original value and record whether the call ended with no connection, no text, or no readable response object. If the wait value itself was not recorded, do not guess a default from the Planner object file. We still cannot say whether the wait value changed before the connection attempt, or who populated the different locations in the response.

# Planner and TCP Timeout Troubleshooting Tree

Earlier, this page treated "Planner not found" and "no content after waiting on TCP" as a single troubleshooting entry point because the descriptions provided by callers were all very brief. After reviewing the object files and old records, this combined approach is no longer suitable for continued use: on the Planner side, first determine whether the request is for a collection or a member read; on the TCP side, first determine whether the wait value was supplied by the caller, and whether what is missing after the call ends is the connection, command text, or return representation. The two phenomena may occur at the same time, but neither can substitute for the other's evidence.

`app/objects/c_planner.py` remains the easiest file to reach on the object side. It directly imports `FirstClassObjectInterface`, `BaseObject`, and uses `marshmallow as ma`. This is enough to let the investigation start at the Planner object boundary, but not enough to treat this file as the routing registration location. The previous record treated "seeing the object definition" as evidence that the member entry point existed, which was too broad; normal object construction, inheritance, and serialization do not mean that both collection and member forms at the request layer can be handled.

## 2023-03 Original Assessment Retained

The original page contains the sentence: "Member lookup failures are mostly because the object was not loaded." At the time, it was only a working hypothesis, not a conclusion. It is retained now because some old troubleshooting habits still start here; but it can no longer be treated as a stopping condition. At a minimum, a member-read failure may also be related to the member identifier supplied by the caller, whether the request reached the API layer, and whether the collection and member entry points were both affected by the same round of changes. The existing records do not contain a complete call chain, so none of these can be written down as the confirmed cause.

The original page also recommended retrying on the TCP side first, then looking back at Planner if there was still no content. That order should likewise be retained as the old guidance, rather than continued as an operating procedure. If there is content after the retry, that only shows that the caller received some kind of content on that call; it does not show that the member read is necessarily unrelated. If there is no content after the retry, that also cannot show that the Planner object was not loaded. The wait on TCP and the Planner member read are two distinct observation entry points.

## Three Items to Fill In First During On-Call

When receiving a Planner-related description, first add the request category, member identifier, and whether the request was seen at the API layer. None of the three needs to be inferred from the object: the request category comes from the caller's actual read action; the member identifier comes from that input; whether the request was received at the API layer comes from the records available at the time. If any one is missing, the record should stop at "cannot yet triage"; do not write it as a missing route or an object-loading failure.

When a collection read returns a response, retain it as a limited-scope counterexample. It can refute the broad claim that "all Planner requests are unavailable," but it cannot prove that member reads exist, that the member identifier did not change, or that the member object can necessarily be retrieved. When a collection read returns no response, first check whether the request reached the API layer; if it did not, do not continue digging through the object's inheritance hierarchy.

The identifier for a member read cannot be casually picked from the list as a substitute. When the incident report says "opening a certain Planner does not work," first ask the caller to provide the original identifier. If the identifier is unknown, continuing to trace object loading will only disguise missing input as a technical finding. If the identifier is known but no such request was seen at the API layer, return to request construction and possible identifier conversion; even then, the failure should not be called an object-loading failure.

## One Lookup That Did Not Pan Out

During review, we once started from the object adjacency of `c_planner.py` to look for the send site of TCP, hoping to use a single call path to explain both the member read and the wait anomaly. This approach yielded no direct connection. The file provides dependencies and declarations near the Planner object; it does not show where the TCP call is initiated, nor where the wait value is used before the connection attempt.

This attempt produced no evidence that could be followed further, so the TCP branch should not be attached under Planner object loading. This section is retained to prevent someone from later starting again from the object file and interpreting failure to find the TCP location as a "Planner-side anomaly." When the direct call site cannot be found, stop at the gap between the object side and the connection side, and hand the next step back to the side that owns the call records.

Another premature judgment was: if the collection read can proceed, write "Planner routing is normal." This also did not hold up. Collections and members are different request forms; a collection response only shows that the collection side did not stall on that call. The identifier used for the member read, whether the request arrived, and the object-processing result still need to be confirmed separately. In the old records, "routing is normal" should henceforth be understood only as "the collection side was available at that time."

## Branching After Review

```text
Planner-related issue received
|
+-- Collection read
|   |
|   +-- No request seen at the API layer
|   |   `-- Stop at the path from the caller to API; do not inspect object loading
|   |
|   +-- Request seen at the API layer and a response received
|   |   `-- Record the collection side as available; open a separate branch for the member issue
|   |
|   `-- Request seen at the API layer but no response received
|       `-- Save the response form and the object conditions at the time, then examine collection handling
|
+-- Member read
|   |
|   +-- Member identifier unknown
|   |   `-- Ask the caller to provide the input; do not guess a default name
|   |
|   +-- Identifier known, but no request seen at the API layer
|   |   `-- Check request construction and identifier conversion
|   |
|   `-- Identifier known and request seen at the API layer
|       `-- Then check collection, the member entry point, and member-object handling
|
`-- Request type unknown
    `-- Retain the original description; do not continue attributing a cause
```

This tree does not require obtaining the complete call chain first. It only requires first avoiding three common premature jumps: using a successful collection read to certify a successful member read; using the existence of the object file to certify the existence of the route; and using a member-read failure to certify the TCP wait anomaly. Each step only needs to be recorded far enough to determine the next step. Only when the member identifier is clear and the request has in fact reached the API layer is there reason to continue checking whether the collection and member entry points were covered together.

## TCP Side Note

In the TCP branch, `timeout` is input that, when supplied by the caller, must be recorded exactly as given. Preserve this value first, then confirm whether it reaches the connection attempt; if the original value is unavailable, record that the input is missing rather than infer a default from the wait duration. The earlier page treated "waiting a long time" as a sign that the wait value was ineffective; this statement is too broad, and there is currently no evidence to support it.

The "no content" at the end of a call also needs to be broken down. A connection not being established, no command text after the connection, and the caller receiving an object but reading no content lead to different directions for follow-up investigation. Do not collapse them here into the same empty response. If the caller has already obtained JSON, the record should state whether `response` appeared and whether it contained any text; having no object and having an empty field are not the same thing.

The following two still-unconfirmed points remain at the end of the page: whether the member identifier retains its original value after caller processing; whether the error connection path can always produce the same return object. They do not prevent first triaging the collection, member, and TCP, but they must not be prematurely ruled out by the old object-loading assumption.
