# Planner and TCP Timeout Troubleshooting Tree

This page still retains two very old entry points: "Planner cannot be found" and "No content after waiting for TCP". Early incident reports often put them in the same sentence, because all the caller ultimately saw was a read that did not yield the expected content. This shared symptom does not imply a shared cause. In later reviews, the most likely source of misdiagnosis was not any single field, but collapsing collection reads, member reads, connection waits, and response representations into a single "Planner timeout".

The old entry points have not been removed from this page. Old links and old on-call notes still lead people here, and deleting the original wording would prevent later reviews from identifying the step at which an object boundary was mistaken for a request boundary. The current sequence is to separate the requests first, then record the inputs and responses; only when a direct call relationship is observed during the incident are the Planner branch and the TCP branch handled as part of the same chain.

## 2023-03: The Note Originally Left Beside the Object File

The earliest record starts with `app/objects/c_planner.py`. The file header shows `os` and `marshmallow as ma`, and imports `FirstClassObjectInterface` from `app.objects.interfaces.i_object` and `BaseObject` from `app.utility.base_object`. At the time, this was seen as a sufficiently practical starting point: when there was a problem with a member read, first check whether the Planner object could be constructed; if the object existed, assume that collection and member reads should recover together.

There was a leap in this reasoning that was not documented at the time. The object relationships in the file can help locate Planner's object-side definitions, base object relationships, and possible serialization boundaries, but they cannot by themselves explain where HTTP requests are received, nor whether collection requests and member requests enter the request layer separately. The object file is a navigation point here, not a routing table.

The original note also said: "A member lookup failure is most likely caused by the object not being loaded." The original wording is retained so that the old incident context remains understandable; it is not the current conclusion on how to handle the issue. At the time, no record from a single incident captured collection reads, member identifiers, and whether requests were received at the API layer together, so this judgment was neither confirmed nor immediately refuted by a clear counterexample.

The same page also had an even cruder recommendation: "If TCP produces no result, retry, and if there is still no result, check Planner." It conflated connection attempts, command text, and the response read by the caller into a "result". This sentence later sent the investigation on a detour through the object file, without answering where the wait value came from or explaining whether member requests had actually reached the request layer. The original sentence has not been deleted, and the old handling sequence is in the appendix below; from this point onward, it is no longer followed.

## 2023-03: The minimal triage possible at the time

The initial draft did not require filling in the full call chain all at once, only breaking down the incident description enough to avoid immediately misleading the next person handling it. On the Planner side, first ask whether this is a list read or a read of a specific member; on the TCP side, first ask whether the caller supplied a wait value. Without answers to these two questions, continuing to read object definitions would only produce seemingly specific guesses.

```text
Received "Planner cannot be found"
├─ Known to be a collection read
│  ├─ Response received: record the response format
│  └─ No response: confirm whether the request reached the API layer
├─ Known to be a member read
│  ├─ Identifier unknown: go back to the caller for the original input
│  └─ Identifier known: record that identifier, do not substitute a name from the list
└─ Request type unknown
   └─ Keep the original description, stop attributing a cause

Received "A long wait with no content"
├─ Caller supplied a wait value
│  └─ Preserve the original value first
└─ No wait value
   └─ Record the missing input, do not guess the default value
```

This triage was incomplete at the time, but it already avoided two unnecessary actions: immediately declaring member reads to be working normally when a collection read succeeded, and picking a name on the fly from the object list to keep investigating when the member identifier was missing. The former overstated what the observation on the collection side meant, while the latter changed the input from the incident. Both approaches would make it impossible to correlate subsequent logs with the caller's description.

Initially, "whether the API layer received the request" was not yet a required field. At the time, the habit was to go straight to investigating object loading as soon as an object file was seen. Looking back at the old paper notes, this was precisely why member issues were first attributed to the object side: the request might not have arrived yet, or it might have arrived without reaching member handling, but the records contained no observations that could distinguish the two.

## 2023-07: Additional on-call notes

The later marginal notes did not try to rewrite the initial draft, but only added two more actionable statements. The first was: when a collection read returns something, do not use that to vouch for member reads. The second was: when the source of the member identifier is unclear, do not guess a default name and continue. These are narrower than the conclusion that "the object did not load", and closer to the facts that can be recorded during an incident.

The member identifier here is the value that the caller passes to the member read. It is not the text displayed on the page, nor is it the first item picked on the fly from the collection results while on call. If the incident notes only say "a particular Planner is missing", first add the request category and the original identifier. Without these two items, any conclusion that "the member entry point is missing", "the object did not load" or "TCP is making the request hang" lacks a sufficient basis.

The same supplementary note also separately circled TCP's `timeout`. The "wait a long time" wording in the on-call description cannot replace the actual input. When the caller provides a wait value, save the original value, then confirm along the call boundary whether it reaches the connection attempt; when the caller provides no wait value, this page records only missing input and does not fill in a number that merely looks reasonable based on the final wait time.

At the time, someone thought that a long wait alone was enough to show that the wait value had not been used. That statement was not retained as a conclusion. Wait time is affected at multiple points, including whether the connection is established, whether post-connection processing finishes, and when the caller reads the returned object. Without the original input and connection-side records, a perceived wait cannot be written up as evidence that the wait value was rewritten.

## 2023-07: First follow-up trace that did not pan out

During review, we once started from `c_planner.py` and followed object adjacency to find the send site for TCP, hoping to use the same call path to explain the member-read and wait anomalies. The search did not pan out. The object file presents Planner's local declarations, base-object relationships, and serialization dependencies; it does not show where the TCP call originates, nor where the wait value is passed to the connection attempt.

Once the search failed to yield a direct relationship, it should have stopped and left the TCP branch at the call boundary. In fact, the old record continued by writing a section following the sequence "fix Planner first, then look at TCP". This sequence is a trace left by a failed attempt, not a runtime relationship confirmed later. It shows that, at the time, code adjacency was mistakenly treated as runtime ownership.

That same review also contained another judgment that did not hold: because the collection read could return, it wrote "Planner routing is normal". That statement applies only to that one collection-side call. Collection and member are two different request forms; a collection returning cannot prove that the member identifier was unchanged, that the member request arrived, or that member processing can complete. Since the materials from that round did not preserve the original input for the member call, no further determination can be made.

To prevent old records from being misread, within this page "routing is normal" will henceforth retain only one narrow meaning: the collection-side request returned a result in that call. It is no longer a conclusion about the entire Planner request boundary, nor a prerequisite for the TCP branch.

## 2023-07-31: Revised wording from the review feedback

During review, it was required to explicitly correct the inference that "the existence of an object means the entry point exists." An object definition can indicate what exists at the object layer, but cannot by itself indicate what has been registered at the request layer. This correction is not intended to invalidate the value of `c_planner.py`; it remains the starting point for checking object boundaries, inheritance relationships, and serialization adjacency. What needs to be corrected is the leap directly from that file to the conclusion that the member request has been received.

The review also requires the meaning of "empty" in TCP to be broken down explicitly. If the connection has not been established, the call has not yet obtained a usable connection; if the connection has been established but the command has no text, content after the connection is missing; only when the caller has obtained a return object but reads an empty field is it an observation about the returned representation. These three phenomena may ultimately all be described as "no content," but the place to investigate next differs.

The old page did not distinguish these three locations, so "an empty response is just a timeout" was also marked as a diagnostic statement that no longer applies. A missing return object, a missing corresponding key in the object, and a key that exists but whose value is an empty string must not all be labeled with the same term. When writing a record, first state which one was observed; do not give a cause first.

The review left one question open and did not require filling it in with speculation: whether the member identifier still has its original value after caller-side processing. The existing material only supports saying that, when the identifier is unknown, one should go back to the caller for the missing input; if the API layer does not see a member request, review the request construction and identifier conversion. The material is insufficient to say that the conversion definitely occurs in a particular object file or fixed interface.

## Old sequence previously given to on-call (deprecated)

The tree below preserves the original handling logic. It was once used to narrow the scope quickly, so it was not removed from the documentation; however, every branch expanded a local observation into a broader conclusion and must no longer be used as current procedure.

```text
Retry TCP first
├─ Has content
│  └─ Assume Planner is unrelated
└─ No content
   └─ Open the Planner object file
      ├─ Can see the object definition
      │  └─ Assume the member entry point exists
      └─ Cannot see the expected object
         └─ Assume redeployment is required
```

The first problem is that a retry of TCP with content does not indicate that member reading is unrelated. A retry is merely a new call observation; it cannot be used to overwrite the state of another type of request. The second problem is that the object file's existence does not mean that the request layer has already processed the member entry point. The third problem is that not seeing the expected content also does not naturally imply that redeployment is required; the incident may still be missing the request category, member identifier, request-arrival record, or original wait value.

Another less obvious side effect of the old sequence is that it encourages the handler to first look for an object that can explain all the phenomena. The member read and the TCP wait are then forced onto the Planner object, and subsequent records contain only "fixed the object" or "retried the connection," losing the request type and input. Keeping this tree is meant to show that old links entering this page should bypass it, not because it can still be used for the current judgment.

## 2024 year-end cleanup: classify by observation location first

When this page was organized later, the reported observations were first divided into three categories. This was not to write up every issue as a separate incident, but to avoid filling gaps in one branch with causal inferences drawn from another. Collection reads, member reads, and TCP calls may all occur during the same release verification; each category should still retain its own minimal record.

```text
Reported observations
|
+-- "The list has no content"
|   `-- Collection-read behavior
|
+-- "The list has content, but the specified member cannot be read"
|   `-- Member-read behavior
|
+-- "No expected text or return value after waiting"
    `-- TCP call and return-handling behavior
```

Collection reads must record at least two things: whether the request reached the API layer, and whether that request returned anything. If the request did not arrive, stop at the path from the caller to API; examining object loading at this point will not answer why the request did not arrive. If the request arrived but returned nothing, save the return shape and object state at the time, then examine collection-side processing. If the request returned something, record it as an observation of collection-side availability, and do not elevate it to proof that the member branch succeeded.

Member reads require one more item to be recorded: where the member identifier came from. If the identifier is unknown, stop making inferences and go back to the caller to obtain the original input. If the identifier is known but the API layer has no request for that member, examine request construction and possible transformation points; do not substitute "the object was not loaded" for the fact that the request has not yet arrived. Only when the identifier is known and the API layer has already seen the request should you check whether the collection and member entry points both exist, and whether processing of the member object has completed.

The minimal record for the TCP branch also has three layers. The first layer is whether the caller supplied a wait value; if there is no original value, stop assessing whether passthrough occurred. The second layer is whether the connection attempt has been confirmed; if the original value exists but the connection side has no record, investigate the path from the wait value to the connection attempt, and do not work backward from the final return. The third layer is what the caller actually received: no object, an object missing a key, or a key that is present but has empty text.

This classification does not require tracing every anomaly to its root cause. Its purpose is to first put verifiable observations in the right place. Continuing to dig through object code when the member identifier is unknown will only disguise missing input as an object failure; continuing to compare responses when the original wait value for TCP is missing also cannot answer whether that value was passed through unchanged. The stopping conditions are kept conservative because the old page has already demonstrated that merging too early creates incorrect conclusions that are harder to clean up.

## Current Troubleshooting Tree

```text
Received an exception related to Planner or TCP
|
+-- Can the request type be determined?
|   |
|   +-- Collection read
|   |   |
|   |   +-- No request seen at the API layer
|   |   |   `-- Stop at the path from the caller to API; do not check object loading
|   |   |
|   |   +-- A request was seen at the API layer and a response was returned
|   |   |   `-- Record it as available on the collection side; if there are still issues, switch to the member or TCP branch
|   |   |
|   |   `-- A request was seen at the API layer but no response was returned
|   |       `-- Record the response shape and object conditions, then check collection handling
|   |
|   +-- Member read
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Member identifier unknown
|   |   |   `-- Ask the caller to provide the original identifier; stop inferring
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Identifier known, no member request seen at the API layer
|   |   |   `-- Check request construction and identifier conversion; do not write this up as an object-loading failure
|   |   |
|   |   `-- Identifier known, a member request was seen at the API layer
|   |       `-- Check the collection and member entry points, then check member-object handling
|   |
|   +-- Call to TCP
|   |   |
|   |   +-- No original text for the awaited value
|   |   |   `-- Record that the input is missing; stop deciding whether it was passed through
|   |   |
|   |   +-- An awaited value exists, but the connection attempt is unconfirmed
|   |   |   `-- Trace the path from that value to the connection attempt; do not infer backward from the return
|   |   |
|   |   +-- The connection attempt has ended, but the text is missing
|   |   |   `-- Record the connection, command text, and return fields separately
|   |   |
|   |   `-- The caller has obtained the returned object
|   |       `-- Record the object, key, and value; do not conflate an empty string with no object
|   |
|   `-- Request type unknown
|       `-- Preserve the original description; do not enter a specific branch
|
`-- Planner and TCP appear simultaneously
    `-- Save the two sets of records separately; merge them only after a direct call relationship is found
```

The stopping point for the collection branch is "whether the request reached the API layer." If there is no such request, whether the collection object can be constructed is not the current question. If the request has arrived and a response was returned, there is no need to fabricate an explanation of a member failure on the collection side; the member branch should use its own identifier and request record. If the request has arrived but there is no response, the record should retain that instance's response form and object conditions, so that later it does not consist of only one sentence: "The list is empty."

The key to the member branch is not to first determine whether the object exists, but to retain the member identifier. Only when the identifier is known and the request has arrived is it worth checking whether the request layer simultaneously covers the collection and member forms. When the identifier is unknown, even if the collection side has returned a response, a name from it cannot be used as the original input. Doing so would change the problem itself and conceal whether the caller lost or changed the identifier during conversion.

When Planner and TCP are abnormal at the same time, at least two sets of records must be retained. The Planner set must include at least the request category, whether the member identifier is known, and whether the API layer saw the request; the TCP set must include at least whether a wait value exists, whether the connection attempt was confirmed, and the response form received by the caller. Once both sets of records are complete, if a direct call relationship can still be found, continue investigating them as one incident; when there is no such relationship, do not write it as a unified "routing timeout."

## Current registration checkpoint

The requirements checked by the current implementation are: `PlannerApi` registers GET `/planners` and GET `/planners/{planner_id}` with the same aiohttp registry; the collection and member routes must coexist, and the member parameter name must remain planner_id.

This checkpoint is used only when the member identifier is known and the API layer has indeed seen the member request. It does not require the collection and member to share the same object handling, and it does not allow collection success to substitute for evidence that the member path exists. If the registration record shows only one entry, record the missing entry; if both entries exist, return to the member identifier, request construction, and member object handling, and do not continue calling the issue a "collection route anomaly."

The requirement for the same registry also does not mean that all Planner symptoms can be resolved at the registration point. When the registration records are complete, no collection response may still require looking at collection handling; no member result may still require checking the input or object handling. Its purpose here is to rule out a clear request-boundary gap, not to uniformly classify all member read failures as routing problems.

An old page mixed object-file checks with entry-point checks because those two stopping points had not been clearly defined at the time. The object-side investigation can still start from `app/objects/c_planner.py`: inspect the object boundary containing Planner, the adjacency relationships between `FirstClassObjectInterface` and `BaseObject`, and the serialization-related `marshmallow as ma`. But after seeing this content, return to the request branch to decide whether to continue, rather than working backward and claiming that the collection and member entry points have already been verified.

## TCP Waiting and Return Representation

The TCP branch does not use the Planner object's state to explain the wait. When the caller supplies `timeout`, first save its original value, then trace downward to confirm whether that value enters the connection attempt. Whether any conversion occurs in between should be determined from the actual call records; if the original value is unavailable, still terminate with missing input. A long wait only shows that the caller experienced waiting; it cannot by itself show that the supplied value was invalid, replaced, or ignored.

After the connection attempt ends, record the command text and the returned object separately. The TCP session command's JSON return carries the command text via `response`. At minimum, the troubleshooting record must state whether the caller has an object, whether the key appears, and, if it does, whether it contains text. No object, no such key in the object, and a key that exists but has empty text may all appear to the caller as "no content," but they are not the same observed situation.

Here, empty text is not automatically interpreted as connection failure. When the connection has not been established, the focus is on whether a usable connection was obtained; when the connection is established but the command has no text, the focus is on the content after connection; when the caller obtains an object but its field is empty, the focus is on the return representation. Older records grouped all of these situations under "response is empty," which is no longer sufficient to support subsequent decisions.

If the incident record contains only the last prompt the caller saw, the flow of the waiting value cannot be inferred backward from that prompt. If it contains only the connection attempt, it also cannot show whether the member request was fully registered. Filling out the TCP branch and the Planner branch to the minimum record for each, and only then examining their relationship, ensures that later supplementary material can still be put back in the correct place.

## Two Approaches Not Adopted in One Meeting

In one retrospective, someone proposed that, when the collection entry point is stable, the caller could retry reading the member on its own. This approach was not adopted. It would allow the caller to mask problems with the member identifier or member entry point; subsequent records would contain only the retry count and lose the original request category. Collection readability should be preserved as a narrowly scoped observation, not used as a reason for the member branch to remain silent.

Another suggestion was to label all TCP exceptions as "Invalid wait value". This suggestion was also not adopted. Whether the wait value was received, whether it was passed unchanged into the connection attempt, whether text was produced after the connection, and whether the caller received the corresponding fields are sequential but distinct checkpoints. When the original input is unavailable, only record that the input is missing; when connection-side information is unavailable, only record that the connection side is unconfirmed.

The meeting also left a related question open: whether the member identifier retains its original value after processing by the caller. There is currently not enough evidence to attribute this issue to the Planner object, request registration, or TCP processing. This question does not block the basic triage above; however, if the collection contains data, the member identifier looks reasonable, and the API layer still has not seen a member request, record the point where the caller performs the conversion as a separate observation.

## Items Not Split Out

It is still unconfirmed whether connection paths involving exceptions can always construct the same return object. The available evidence is insufficient to establish that different exceptions all leave the same `response` structure, or that the caller reads fields in the same way on every path. Therefore, whenever an object or key is missing during troubleshooting, record the actual point where it is missing rather than replacing it with a single "Response is empty" entry.

It is also still unconfirmed whether there is an additional adaptation layer between member identifiers and object processing. Having a known identifier and a request that reaches the API layer only means that registration and member processing can be checked; it does not mean that object loading necessarily succeeded, nor does it mean that the identifier did not change at an earlier point. If evidence from the same call becomes available later, append it after the input and arrival records for the member branch, rather than folding it back into the initial object-loading assumption.

Migration materials related to the shared time format with second-level precision are located separately at DOC-14. This entry for a related topic is not part of the Planner registration assessment on this page, nor is it used to explain the TCP wait. It is retained only to prevent people arriving from the same round of compatibility checks from writing time-format issues into the troubleshooting records for member routing.

## Old Appendix: Two-Line Shorthand

An old on-call note once condensed the issues into the following two lines:

```text
Cannot open member: Check whether Planner is loaded.
TCP has no result: Increase the wait and try again.
```

Both lines are retained as historical starting points, but neither is still applicable. The first line omitted whether the request was actually a collection read or a member read, where the member identifier came from, and whether the API layer saw the request. The second line omitted the wait value passed in by the caller, whether the connection attempt had ended, and the distinction between the return object and the text.

When an old link shows you only these two lines, you should not modify the object directly or repeatedly retry the connection. First return to the current triage tree: supply the missing input when the member identifier is unknown, check the inbound path when no request is seen at the API layer; stop at the caller when the wait value is missing, then distinguish the return forms by object, key and value after the connection ends. The old shorthand can explain the processing pressure at the time, but it can no longer serve as the basis for decisions in the current investigation.

versions.body:
# Ability and Object Interface Decision

This record preserves a requirement-classification decision made around R2026.09; it is not the current interface description. It originally placed "Ability Full CRUD Route Matrix" and "Data/Knowledge Shared Object Service API" under the same regression memo, for a very practical reason: both sides were asking how objects are retrieved, modified, or saved, and both were treated as compatibility gaps in the schedule. During later review, this juxtaposition was still useful, but the original explanation relied too heavily on `app/objects/c_ability.py`, so it is not suitable as a basis for judging the current implementation.

## Judgments retained in the initial draft

The initial draft's decision did not claim that the two object systems already shared a single implementation; it only decided not to combine them into one task. The Ability track focused on whether resource entry points separately left operation surfaces for collections and individual objects; the Data/Knowledge track focused on whether the service abstraction could support saving and retrieving objects. If the latter were treated as an internal detail of the former, routing gaps would be hidden by "the object already exists"; if, conversely, the route table were treated as the service boundary, interface ownership would be incorrectly written as a matter for the HTTP layer.

A more expedient approach was discussed at the time: center on the inheritance relationships in the Ability file, list all potentially relevant object services, and add routes outward from there. This approach was not adopted. `c_ability.py` does indeed show `FirstClassObjectInterface`, and it directly introduces `collections`, `os`, and `marshmallow as ma`, but these details only show that the file is a local observation point at the object layer. They cannot show that the Data and Knowledge service interfaces are aligned, nor prove that every Ability operation has a corresponding resource route.

Therefore, the initial draft left two independent verification areas:

| Verification area | Content retained by the decision at the time | Content not decided in this record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ability | Whether operation surfaces for collections and individual Abilities exist separately | Which API class or route registration contains the concrete implementation |
| Data/Knowledge | The shared object service interface must have call evidence from both successful and failed cases | The complete compatibility scope of each backend |

This table is the troubleshooting split from that time, not the current module map. In particular, "complete CRUD" has always been a name pending verification here; it does not mean that the initial draft had already seen the complete matrix.

## Why they were not merged at the time

The merged approach had two appealing aspects. First, both topics contain the word "object", so putting them in one table looks convenient for handoff. Second, the object inheritance relationships in the Ability file make it easy to think that the interface issue can be explained all the way from the model file to the service layer. After review, they were still kept separate, mainly because they face different failure modes.

The failure mode on the Ability side is a missing or asymmetric resource operation surface: the collection being accessible does not mean that modification and deletion of a specified object necessarily have entry points; an individual resource being readable does not mean that the remaining operations have been arranged in the same way. The failure mode on the Data/Knowledge side is instead inconsistent expectations at the two ends of a call about the shared abstraction: a call reaching a service does not mean that object saving, reading, and failure handling use constraints at the same layer. The former requires checking routes and object identifiers, while the latter requires retaining evidence from the call itself.

The initial draft once said, "The base class of Ability objects is sufficient as the common basis for both tracks." This statement should now be considered outdated. It conflated code adjacency with the service contract. It is retained to explain why the two topics were paired at the time, not to let future maintainers continue from that premise.

Another abandoned approach was to put all relevant objects directly into one release checklist. This would make the regression page look complete, but it would not answer where to return when a failure occurs: check the resource entry point first, or the service abstraction first. The decision remains to retain two follow-up paths and allow both to be incomplete in the same release. The cost is a less tidy record; the benefit is that evidence from one direction will not be borrowed for the other.

## What the file entry left behind

`app/objects/c_ability.py` has a very narrow purpose in this record: it is the entry point to which the old investigation was directed by the issue name and call name. The dependencies visible in the file header are enough to remind the reviewer that Ability belongs to the object-layer context and that the object is adjacent to `FirstClassObjectInterface`. Beyond that, the page does not treat this path as the route implementation location, nor as the service-definition location for Data or Knowledge.

Earlier records phrased "start from the object file" as if it were a fixed sequence. That wording should also be withdrawn. An object file can help confirm terminology and adjacency, but it cannot replace checking resource endpoints; likewise, evidence from a successful or failed service call cannot be replaced by an object model file. The old entry remains because it explains why the investigation at the time converged on Ability, not because it covers every issue.

For later follow-up, the original decision only requires first distinguishing which object is being asked about:

- If the question is whether a particular Ability has a corresponding resource operation surface, inspect the collection and the specified object separately;
- If the question is whether Data/Knowledge shares an object service interface, return to the service calls and separately record what is observed on success and failure;
- If a clue only leads back to `c_ability.py`, it can only supplement the Ability object context and cannot complete confirmation for the other track.

These three points are the work boundary left at the time; they do not constitute runtime steps and are not guaranteed to apply to later module splits.

## Later card addenda

After CAL-206 was created, the card treated Ability Full CRUD Route Matrix separately as an inventory of reconstructable incident evidence and required the corresponding module maintainer to verify current-version behavior and an entry point that could be checked further. This is consistent with the initial split decision: the card did not require inferring routes from the shared object service interface, nor did it treat the object file as a conclusion.

The card later went through status changes for security triage and starting work. These changes are retained here because they show that the Ability track moved from a classification issue in the old memo into actual verification; they do not show that verification has been completed, much less that the original "complete" state has been proven. Some readers previously understood starting work to mean that the matrix had been closed out; that understanding is not valid.

CAL-223 instead placed Data/Knowledge Shared Object Service API in supplementary regression for user-side scenarios, requiring one successful call and one failed call to leave separately observable results. It was later categorized under release processing and work began on it. The card's wording further confirms that the material for this track should come from call evidence, rather than being extracted from the Ability object's inheritance relationships. The card did not provide general definitions of the two service interfaces, nor did it supplement this decision with the complete compatibility scope.

The appearance of the two cards changed this document's purpose: the initial draft only split the problem apart; after the addenda, readers could separately find the Ability incident-evidence inventory and the Data/Knowledge call records. They still should not be read as two chapters of the same requirement. When provenance or factual sources need to be compared, see also DOC-17; that material is not responsible for filling in route or service-layer conclusions that were not obtained here.

## Decision after this review

Retain the original core decision: the Ability routing matrix and Data/Knowledge Shared Object Service API are parallel compatibility verification areas, and their judgments cannot be combined merely because their names are similar or they are adjacent at the object layer. The old Ability file entry continues to serve as a follow-up point for terminology and object adjacency; the evidence for Data/Knowledge continues to be based on successful and failed call evidence.

At the same time, withdraw the stronger implication in the initial draft: the appearance of `FirstClassObjectInterface` is no longer treated as evidence that the two service interfaces are shared, nor as corroborating evidence that CRUD is covered. This correction does not negate the value of the file's existence; it only narrows its interpretive scope in this record.

One question not yet moved elsewhere is whether, when the Ability resource-operation check finds a gap, it should also require recording failure evidence at the object service layer. The existing material provides no such linkage rule. For now, continue keeping evidence separately along the two tracks to avoid prematurely fixing the attribution of the gap.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Record separately" as split
    state "Ability route verification" as ability
    state "Data/Knowledge service verification" as data
    state "Object file entry" as file
    state "Successful and failed call evidence" as calls
    [*] --> split
    split --> ability
    split --> data
    ability --> file
    data --> calls
```

## Retained old sticky note

> Old wording: Since Ability is an object, the routing matrix and service interface can be handled along the same follow-up path.
>
> Later correction: Object relationships can only explain why the two items appeared in the same round of compatibility discussion; they cannot replace separate verification of resource entry points and service calls.

This note was not deleted because it identifies the point most likely to be misread in the initial draft. If later material only mentions CAL-206, it should be understood as navigation for the Ability track; if it only mentions CAL-223, it should be understood as navigation for the Data/Knowledge regression evidence. Only when both are mentioned does it indicate that this page's historical classification may still be relevant.

# Operation and Multipart Compatibility Migration

This migration moves the compatibility checks previously scattered alongside interface changes into a single check centered on the Operation object. The first place to look is `app/objects/c_operation.py`: handle the report resource entry point and the encryption and encoding parameters for Multipart requests in the same round of changes. The goal is not to change report content, but to avoid leaving two sets of logic by changing the route first and adding the parameters later.

## Migration Scope

The old checks tracked report resources and Multipart separately. After the migration, first confirm that report requests on Operation can still go through the existing object. Once that is confirmed, bring the existing Multipart encryption and encoding options into the same request construction code. When parameters are not explicitly provided, do not supply defaults here or add separate encoding in the report branch.

The old convention used here centralizes compatibility handling for both report resources and Multipart at the Operation object layer. Callers only need to use the original Operation entry point; they do not need to keep a separate parameter assembly path for report requests.

## Procedure

1. Keep the existing Operation request entry point first, and only move the report resource checks alongside that object; do not change the displayed content at the same time.
2. Check that Multipart requests still carry the encryption and encoding parameters. Pass both parameters downstream as supplied, leaving them absent when they are missing.
3. Once report resource access works, inspect requests carrying Multipart data. If differences appear with both changes in place, first back out the parameter assembly changes, but keep the migrated entry point for report resources.
4. Do not treat the encryption output as part of the report output. The report side only checks whether the resource was retrieved; the Multipart side only checks whether supplied parameters were lost along the way.

## Restoring the Old Path

If, after combining the checks, you cannot tell whether differences come from report resources or Multipart parameters, return to handling them separately: check report resources through Operation's old entry point, and trace Multipart parameters separately from request construction. When restoring the old path, do not change existing Operation data or overwrite the original input values with re-encoded data.

At the time, putting both checks at the same object layer was thought to reduce omissions, so the migration did not retain any additional boundary markers between report resources and Multipart parameters. If this record is still needed for later troubleshooting, start with request construction in `app/objects/c_operation.py`, then decide whether to split the checks into two tracks.

## Assessments from the initial draft

This record covers two items that came up together but should not be combined into a single conclusion: Executor Path Update Queue, and the fallback when an Operation result file is missing. The early investigation used the terms agent object, executor, and value to locate `app/objects/c_agent.py`. The file header shows `import re`, `from base64 import b64decode`, `from datetime import datetime`, and `from urllib.parse import urlparse`; these only identify a starting point for review and local dependencies. On their own, they do not establish when the queue takes effect or which fields the response retains when result is missing.

The working hypothesis at the time was that path changes were first retained as pending changes on the executor; reading a new value was not enough to conclude that the active execution entry point had finished switching over. Operation result was treated as a separate compatibility path: if the file was missing, a fallback might be needed to let callers continue to identify the operation link, rather than applying the path-update reasoning to it.

The initial draft did not describe either hypothesis as released behavior. A targeted review through the existing entry points was still needed, retaining inputs, outputs, and the results immediately before and after the path update. # Executor and Result Fallback Decisions

## First, Preserve Two Investigation Contexts

This page did not start as a complete design, but as a note separating two issues that can easily turn up along the same investigation path. One issue is called Executor Path Update Queue, and the other is called Operation result Missing File Fallback. Both may be seen at the same operation-related call site, but the object states differ: the former discusses how a change to an executor is retained, while the latter discusses how an existing operation link is read when the result file is unavailable. Collapsing the two into "update succeeded" or "result failed" loses the intermediate states.

The entry point has consistently been `app/objects/c_agent.py`. This is not because it can explain the entire control plane on its own, but because the early notes led into this file through local terms such as agent, executor, and value. At the time, the following could be seen at the top of the file:

```python
import re
from base64 import b64decode
from datetime import datetime
from urllib.parse import urlparse
```

These dependencies provided a concrete place to focus the review. `re` indicates that local processing may need to recognize text patterns, `b64decode` makes encoded values another nearby item to inspect, and `datetime` and `urlparse` also place time values and address values near this object. They only indicate what is available at the file's entry point; their names cannot tell us when the Executor update queue is consumed, nor can the handling of URL establish the return protocol for Operation result. This deliberately does not turn a file header into an end-to-end call graph.

The initial draft could support only two lines of reasoning. A path value and a path taking effect are not the same thing; reading a new value only indicates that the object carries that value, not that execution still using the old path has ended, nor that subsequent actions have obtained the new path. The other line of reasoning is that, when no result file has been left behind, the entry point for recognizing an Operation link should not disappear simply because the result content cannot be read. At the time, the latter was only a direction for compatibility design, not a confirmed response copied from runtime output.

## Working Assumptions in the Initial Draft

The working hypothesis for path updates is: first retain the change as a pending item, then process it at the existing application point. Viewed this way, "a new path has been discovered" needs to be kept separate from "the new path is already being used for execution". If the value currently used by the Executor is overwritten directly, only a single current value remains at the investigation site, making it hard to tell whether it is the old path, a candidate path, or the new path already in effect. If the path switch happens at another point in time, a failure also cannot be distinguished as "no change" or "the change has been queued but not yet applied".

Directly changing the value does have an apparent benefit: subsequent code only needs to read from one location, the interpretation path is short, and the state also looks clean. But it hides pending changes inside the current object. For this compatibility issue, one fewer intermediate state does not mean one fewer behavioral state. As long as the old entry point might still be used by some action, overwriting it directly removes the point of comparison for later checks.

Keeping changes pending initially comes at the cost of more complex relationship tracking. At a minimum, it must be possible to distinguish the currently visible value from the candidate change, and later to tell whether the change has reached the point where it should be applied. The material on this page does not establish the full set of fields in a queue item, the consumer names, or the persistence location, so no class names, message formats, or fabricated execution sequences have been added. The decision remains at the level of object relationships: when a new value appears, first interpret it as a pending change; without evidence that it has been applied, do not describe the current execution entry point as having already switched.

The choice of how to handle Operation result raises a separate set of issues. Treating a missing file directly as a read error makes the behavior straightforward and avoids producing an empty result that looks successful; however, if the caller already has an operation link, the resource it wants to query may still be the same operation. Combining "no result artifact was left behind" and "the operation resource does not exist" into one error erases this distinction.

Retaining the operation link's display information and providing an empty fallback for the result content is another compatibility approach. It does not claim that the result has been generated, but only allows the query layer to express "the link is still recognizable, and the result content is empty". An empty value here is not proof of successful execution, nor can it be used to fabricate the contents of the missing file. Field names, value types, and the link's display format need to be confirmed through inputs and outputs, and cannot be inferred solely from the problem title.

## Two options before review

For the path issue, the options considered can be distilled into two.

The first is to immediately rewrite the current Executor path. As soon as the path value changes, put the new value in the location currently in use. This approach suits a model in which path changes necessarily take effect immediately, but there is no evidence of such timing in this case. It would also associate the last use of the old path and the first use of the new path with the same value. When an exception occurs, investigators can only guess from the outside whether the change has been processed.

The second is to retain pending path changes. The current value continues to represent the path currently in use or previously visible, while the change waits separately to be applied. It requires clearer state observability, but allows troubleshooting material to preserve the distinction between "the change has been detected" and "the change has been applied". The change history for R2026.09 takes this approach as the basis for the decision, but does not present fields or consumers that were not provided as facts.

These two approaches also have different compatibility costs. Immediately changing the value has a low migration cost, but existing callers might mistake a candidate value for the effective value; the queued approach requires callers to accept an unfinished intermediate state and involves more verification work, but the transition between the old and new paths can be observed. Since this page concerns the evolution of requirements rather than interface field descriptions, the decision settles only this distinction, not the implementation layout in material that has not been provided.

For the result issue, the first option is to propagate an error whenever the file is missing. Its advantage is that failure is explicit, and callers will not mistake an empty value for a result. The disadvantage is that resource identification and result reading are tied together, and the existence of the operation link is obscured by the file's state.

The second option is to continue returning the display identity of link while allowing an empty fallback for result. Its cost is that callers must distinguish empty results from actual results, and tests cannot just check whether the request succeeded. Its benefit is that it preserves the entry point for identifying an existing operation, avoiding turning a result-file issue into a resource-not-found issue. The current decision is to choose the second option for compatibility, while retaining the caveat that "confirmation with actual output is required".

## The entry-point scope has not expanded

The local dependencies of `app/objects/c_agent.py` can help trace back to neighboring objects involving paths, encoding, time, and URL, but they cannot establish the full Executor lifecycle or all the relationships among Operation report routing, storage locations, and callers. File paths are starting points for verification, not conclusions about responsibility. This boundary is important: if an end-to-end conclusion is drawn solely from file locations, any subsequent counterexample, regardless of which layer it falls in, will have already been attributed to the wrong object.

This page therefore does not fill in any job, commit, artifact name, command, filename, or call stack. The intended check recorded in CAL-211 is to trigger the job corresponding to "Executor Path Update Queue" through the existing automation entry point and record the job, commit, and actual artifact name; this indicates that verification needs to bring back the run identity and actual artifacts, but does not indicate that these materials are already present on this page. The intended check in CAL-228 is to run "Operation result Missing File Fallback" through the existing test entry point and record both the affected units and the adjacent unchanged units; this, too, is a starting point for verification, not a completed report.

This scope also explains why `app/objects/c_agent.py` cannot replace all follow-up checks. The direct dependencies in the file header allow someone to start from a local object, but they do not tell us where the queue is consumed or which layer handles missing results. The decision is to preserve the entry point while leaving implementation ownership to be determined by the code and targeted output.

## Counterexamples from subsequent verification

The first item added back in the version history was a caller walkthrough. CAL-211 recorded `caller_walkthrough` on 2025-10-01, and moved into `work_started` the next day. These two actions indicate that verification progressed from the caller entry point toward actual work; they do not amount to a successful end-to-end run. The initial draft's assessment that "verification along the entry point is needed" therefore still stands, but can now be stated more specifically: first examine the calling relationships, then fill in the actual job and artifacts, rather than determining behavior solely from the name of a local object.

CAL-228 added `counterexample_added` on 2025-10-29. This counterexample did not fill in the missing output for this page, but served to prevent the two paths from being used as evidence for each other. Path updates have their own state transitions, and a missing result file has its own read branch; even if they occur in the same operation scenario, a null value in result cannot be used to prove that the path queue has been processed, nor can a change in the path value be used to prove that the result file definitely exists or is definitely missing.

The public comment on 2025-11-03 defined the gap more narrowly: Operation result Missing File Fallback still has one unconfirmed point, and the input and output need to remain in the targeted rerun record. This comment changed the strength of the conclusion, not the direction of the approach. We can now retain the design choice to "handle link identity separately from result content", but cannot claim that this page already includes that input and output, much less fill in the specific response JSON, filename, or error text based on a single comment.

On 2025-11-06, CAL-228 moved to blocked because the account with standard permissions had not yet been enabled. This reflects incomplete verification conditions, not a counterexample to result behavior itself, nor evidence that the Executor path has already failed. If the account is unavailable, all that can be established is that the conditions for observation are blocked; blank output cannot be interpreted as a file-missing result. Permission-related blocking and technical attribution must be kept separate in the records.

These historical materials move this page from "having two reasonable hypotheses" to "having two separately maintained verification branches". But they do not turn unobserved implementation details into facts. What has changed over this history is that the boundaries of the conclusions have become clearer, not that evidence has appeared out of thin air.

## Decisions Retained After Review

As of this version, the decision on path updates is: record and investigate Executor path changes as pending changes. When a new value appears, first determine whether it is a candidate change or an already applied state; without evidence that it has been applied, do not state that the execution entry point has switched. "Pending" here is intended to preserve distinctions between states, not to indicate that this page already knows the queue fields, handlers, or consumption timing.

The decision for Operation result is: when the file is missing, prioritize preserving the operation link's identity for queries and display, and keep an empty fallback as a compatibility option for the result content. This approach does not fabricate results, interpret null values as success, or recast the reason for the missing file as a path update failure. The exact object returned still needs to be confirmed through a targeted rerun.

The two decisions are parallel, not an upstream–downstream causal chain. A path update failure cannot automatically explain a missing result file; nor can a missing result file prove, in reverse, that the path queue did not take effect. A single rerun can observe both phenomena, but the record must document the inputs, outputs, and unknowns for each separately. Otherwise, a combined summary will once again collapse state transitions and result reads into a single anomaly.

The entry point currently retained for investigation is still `app/objects/c_agent.py`. To confirm where the queue is applied, where result is read, or the adjacent callers, continue tracing the code paths from these local object relationships; do not treat the decisions on this page as a call graph. CAL-211 and CAL-228 can help locate the corresponding checks, but cannot replace run artifacts.

## Three Simplifications Rejected During Review

"The new path has appeared, so the switch is complete" was rejected. It conflates object values, queue state, and execution timing, cannot explain cases where an action still uses the old path, and cannot accommodate counterexamples added later. The current wording preserves the distinction between candidate changes and applied changes.

"The file does not exist, so the operation does not exist" was also rejected. It fails to distinguish resource identity from result artifacts. As long as the operation link remains the object being queried, the design should not start by removing the link when the result file is missing; but this does not mean this page already has the object returned by a particular run.

"The standard-permission account has not been enabled, so the fallback approach is wrong" is likewise invalid. Permissions only affect whether inputs and outputs can be observed; they cannot supply an actual response for a missing file, much less establish responsibility for the path queue or result reads. blocked is a verification status and cannot serve as a technical conclusion.

Another, broader formulation was not adopted: determining the entire control plane's behavior based solely on `app/objects/c_agent.py`. `re`, `b64decode`, `datetime` and `urlparse` are only the direct dependencies in the file header. They help locate the local logic, but provide no end-to-end evidence for API routing, queue consumers, or result storage. These names are retained to keep the entry point traceable, not to broaden the file's responsibilities.

## State Diagram

The diagram below shows only the two state boundaries that the decisions on this page are intended to preserve. It does not depict unspecified queue fields, consumers, or the actual execution order; "pending verification" is not a success state either.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Change detected
    Change detected --> Pending change : New value
    Pending change --> Path application pending verification : Waiting for the time to apply
    [*] --> operation_link identifiable
    operation_link identifiable --> result file missing : Result file unavailable
    result file missing --> Empty-result fallback direction : Retain link display information
```

The left side of the diagram is the path update branch. The appearance of a new value only takes the observation as far as "Change detected", and a distinction must still be made between pending and applied. The right side of the diagram is the result-reading branch. Identification of the link is separate from the contents of the result file, and when the file is unavailable, an empty-result slot is retained for compatibility. There is no arrow from either side to the other, because the existing materials do not establish that either can be attributed to the other.

## Where exactly the review should stop

The first step in the next targeted review is to prepare an account with standard permissions that can access the existing automation entry point. If the account is still unavailable, the record should go no further than the input conditions and the reason for the blocker; a lack of output must not be used to fill in a conclusion about result. This stopping point is not a rejection of the technical approach, but a way to avoid recording missing observations as a failure sample.

The path branch requires observing the states from when the old value changes until the pending item is applied, distinguishing at least between "detecting a change" and "applying a change". The job, commit, and actual artifact name should be retained, because the intent of the checks in CAL-211 explicitly calls for these run records. Their values are not provided here, and no trigger commands have been fabricated.

The result branch handles only the case where the result file for one operation link is unavailable, retaining the link display information and the output of the returned result as is. In addition to the missing-file sample, adjacent results whose files exist must be used as controls to confirm that the empty fallback has not been set as the default value for all results. CAL-228 require the affected units and adjacent unchanged units to be retained together; this page therefore considers these two types of materials separately, and does not present "adjacent unchanged" as an already observed result.

The review needs to answer at least five local questions. First, whether the value still in use is directly overwritten when a candidate path value appears. Second, at what point the pending change is consumed. Third, whether the operation link can still be queried when the result file is missing. Fourth, whether the fields and values of the empty fallback are stable. Fifth, whether adjacent results whose files exist remain unchanged.

These questions are not a predefined matrix, nor do they call for filling in combinations that have not been provided. They simply break the current decision down into observable inputs and outputs. If the output differs from "retain link, result is empty", first revise the local decision for the result branch, then assess whether the path queue is actually implicated; do not retract all judgments at once just because the two objects appear in the same operation scenario.

## Compatibility costs and responsibility boundaries

Using pending changes makes callers deal with an intermediate object that does not match the current execution state. This cost cannot be eliminated by directly making the candidate value the current value, or there would be no visible boundary between the last use of the old path and the first application of the new path. On the other hand, if a caller accepts only a path value that takes effect immediately, the review still needs to confirm how it handles pending changes; this page contains no material proving that adjacent callers have already been adapted.

Result fallback also has a clear cost. Returning a link and an empty result can preserve resource identity, but callers must know that an empty value does not mean successful output. If callers display the empty value directly as the execution result, this compatibility approach will still lead to misinterpretation; if callers accept only errors, the ability to identify the operation link will be lost instead. The current material supports only keeping these two states separate, not adding a set of caller-handling rules.

Therefore, the responsibility boundary on this page is not "one file is responsible for all compatibility", but rather to record the object relationships that can be settled: path updates are initially handled as pending changes, and when a result file is missing, the link identity and the slot for an empty result are preserved first. The corresponding code and rerun evidence must account for queue fields, consumption points, the result-reading layer, and callers' final behavior. `app/objects/c_agent.py` remains a starting point for localized verification and cannot be treated as proof of ownership of these unconfirmed areas.

## How the old wording is retained in the new version

The two statements in the first draft have not been deleted: "Path changes initially stay in the pending queue", "A missing result file should not erase the operation link". In this version, the first statement becomes the adopted object-relationship decision; the second remains a direction for compatibility, with the details of the returned object awaiting confirmation through inputs and outputs. Keeping the old wording this way lets readers see where the understanding changed, rather than sanitizing the first draft into a design that was complete and correct from the outset.

The starting point for investigation at `app/objects/c_agent.py` is also retained. Subsequent cards have not replaced it with a broader module list. In CAL-211, `caller_walkthrough` makes the verification sequence start with the caller, while in CAL-228, `counterexample_added` requires the two branches to be recorded separately; they change the verification method and the strength of the conclusions, not the structure of the entire control plane.

What this version adds is not a broader interface commitment, but several specific constraints: without evidence that the change has been applied, do not describe the new value as already switched over; without inputs and outputs, do not claim that the empty fallback is already the actual return value; without permissions, do not describe blocked as a technical failure; without end-to-end evidence, do not make a file location bear responsibility for the full chain. These correspond to path state, result fields, review conditions, and code scope, respectively, and cannot be replaced with a single generalized statement.

The remaining work is to be closed out separately. The Executor path update awaits targeted documentation of the old value, candidate changes, application timing, and actual artifacts; the missing Operation result file awaits as-is documentation of the operation link, empty fallback fields, the missing file, and adjacent results. The two records can come from the same round of work, but their respective inputs, outputs, and unconfirmed items must be kept separate. The current decision goes no further than this.

# Fact Relationship Interface Proposal

The initial draft framed the question as "whether the two resources should be split apart", but this framing was premature. The review should first distinguish object representations, operation entry points, and shapes required for compatibility. Fact and relationship can appear in the same result without having to share a lifecycle; sharing a schema also cannot replace determining who is responsible for modifications.

The earlier investigation led to `app/objects/secondclass/c_relationship.py`. Only a few local details can currently be retained directly: the file imports `marshmallow`, references `BaseObject` from `app.utility.base_object`, and also imports `FactSchema` from `app.objects.secondclass.c_fact`. These dependencies are enough to show that the relationship side needs to handle structures adjacent to Fact; they are not enough to show that relationship is a subordinate field of Fact, or that Fact must receive all relationship changes.

We are no longer using the initial draft's claim that "relationship is an appendage of Fact". The presence of `FactSchema` only proves that a connection exists at the representation layer. It may be used for embedding, conversion, or validation, or it may simply keep some part of the two objects' shapes aligned. Who is responsible for saving, who is responsible for querying, and who defines update actions must still be assessed by looking at where the call starts and the object the user ultimately receives.

## Three Things to Separate in This Review

The first is representation. Similar names cannot determine which information relationship needs in its own right and which content is merely a representation aligned with Fact. If a field comes from a common Fact shape, callers should still be able to see that it belongs to Fact semantics; relationship's own meaning should not be disguised as an ordinary fact attribute either. This way, future changes to either side will not silently change the meaning of the other side's returned results.

The second is operation ownership. A call starting from Fact does not mean Fact must handle the modification; conversely, relationship appearing in a Fact result does not automatically prove that it has an independent write entry point. "Navigating to relationship" and "performing an operation on relationship" need to be recorded separately. The former only shows a visible connection between objects, while only the latter affects the interface boundary.

The third is compatibility costs. If existing consumers treat the Fact shape as the complete representation of relationship, introducing a separate boundary may expose default values or missing fields; if consumers already continue processing based on relationship's own information, forcing it back onto the Fact side will only add wrapping. We are not committing to an amount of migration work at this stage; first reconstruct the actual calls and the results users see when those calls complete.

## Candidate Directions

### A: relationship Retains an Independent Representation

This direction treats `c_relationship.py` as the local home for relationship's representation and object behavior. `FactSchema` is used only when sharing the Fact shape is genuinely necessary; the connection between the two is conveyed through explicit fields or nested results, rather than requiring callers to guess which layer will handle the work on their behalf.

A's advantage is that evolving relationship semantics does not require expanding all Fact entry points. It also fits the limited dependencies currently visible: a shared schema can serve as a connection point without merging the object hierarchies. The cost is having to verify whether existing calls already assume that relationship inherently carries Fact's entire shape. If they do, switching cannot be limited to renaming objects, and a transitional representation that allows the old results to be interpreted must be retained.

A does not require adding a full independent interface immediately. Whether to use an independent object representation and whether to provide an independent operation entry point are separate decisions. Only if a review of calls shows that relationship is identified, read, or modified separately is there reason to continue discussing the form of those entry points; if it is only displayed in Fact results, clearly documenting the display boundary is enough for now.

### B: Fact Handles relationship Operations

This direction is suitable only for a narrower situation: actual calls show that relationship is always merely supplementary information for Fact, with no separable creation, read, or modification scenarios. Callers interact only with Fact, and relationship appears only as a fixed part of Fact. This can reduce the number of entry points, but it also shifts the compatibility costs of relationship evolution back to the Fact side.

B's risk is not the file location, but mistaking "there are few calls at present" for "there is no independent boundary". Once relationship has an independent identity, filtering requirements, or a different pace of change, the Fact entry point must take responsibility for maintaining compatibility for both object types. The current material does not contain enough call records to support this conclusion, so B can remain as an option for comparison, but should not be used as grounds for removing relationship's local representation.

If later investigation finds only read chains starting from Fact, that still does not justify choosing B directly. A read chain only answers how results are organized, not who handles writes. Only when the same set of reconstructable calls also shows that all modifications target Fact as a whole can B move from a candidate to a better-supported direction.

### C: Shared Flat Representation

The initial draft treated this as a convenient option, and it is retained here to explain why it was not adopted outright. A flat representation would make reuse of `FactSchema` most straightforward, but would cram Fact fields, relationship fields, and the rules connecting them into the same layer. Callers get a more compact shape, but maintaining it makes it difficult to adjust either object independently.

C is worth comparing again only if the review proves that the two have no separable creation, read, or modification semantics, and that existing consumers consistently depend on the same complete shape. There is currently no such material. Even if an existing implementation branch uses a nearly flat representation, we should first document which compatibility outcomes it preserves, then decide whether the cost is acceptable.

## Tentative Recommendation

For this round, use A as the tentative direction for review: relationship retains a recognizable object representation; dependencies on Fact are kept, through `FactSchema`, at the points where structure is genuinely shared; do not directly elevate the object conventions of `BaseObject` or the processing details of `marshmallow` into a caller-facing contract.

The focus of this recommendation is not to separate the two completely, but to prevent a vague "nested relationship" from replacing several concrete judgments. At a minimum, call records need to answer: whether the request initially targets Fact, relationship, or a result containing both; whether users can distinguish between the two after the result is returned; and which side receives the action if a change occurs. Read calls that involve no modifications should be marked as unable to establish operation ownership.

One counterexample worth noting separately is that relationship appears in a Fact result, but subsequent logic immediately continues processing based on relationship's own information. This supports retaining an independent representation, but does not necessarily imply an independent write entry point. Another counterexample is a call that starts from Fact but treats only relationship as the target to be changed. Here we need to determine whether Fact is the navigation starting point or the actual operation boundary, rather than looking only at the first path segment.

If the review ultimately finds only schema-level references, the proposal should stop at a representation-level recommendation and should not declare A a complete interface decision. Conversely, only if several distinct calls are found to require the same relationship representation is there reason to stabilize that representation and include the transitional shape as part of the implementation changes.

## Review Points for the Existing Branch

CAL-212 were passed to the current module maintainer after the existing implementation was examined, and later moved into review because the existing branch had been completed. These two records show that the discussion is no longer just about naming: the review needs to compare the branch's actual approach against the narrow boundaries above, point by point. They do not mean the proposal has already been approved.

Prioritize two things during the check. First, whether relationship's local representation is still recognizable, or has inadvertently been squeezed into Fact's ordinary fields. Second, whether use of `FactSchema` has expanded into an implicit proxy for Fact operations. If neither problem has occurred, A can serve as an explanatory framework for the existing implementation; if either has occurred, its impact should be added back to this proposal before deciding whether to accept, adjust, or withdraw it.

The fact that a branch already exists should not be used to infer retroactively that B or C has become the design conclusion. An implementation may address a specific call flow first, but the design still needs to establish whether it changes other calls' understanding of object identity. Review questions should focus on concrete result shapes and specific modification actions, rather than broadly confirming whether Fact and relationship can be returned together.

## Migration and Withdrawal

If the review accepts A, migration should begin with how calls understand the objects, not by first replacing import statements. Calls that only need Fact should continue to handle it as Fact; calls that actually process relationship should explicitly identify the relationship portion. `FactSchema` can continue to be reused, but it cannot serve as a reason to bind the two objects into a single change.

There are two conditions for withdrawal. First, actual calls show that relationship has no independent identity, no independent read or modification scenarios, and all consumers treat it only as a fixed component of Fact; in that case, A would add a layer without benefit, and B should be compared again. Second, the existing branch proves that a single shape is required to preserve current results; in that case, first record the specific compatibility points, then determine whether C is more manageable than extensive adaptation.

What remains unconfirmed is the exact responsibility of `FactSchema` in the relationship file, whether independent relationship operations exist, and which user-visible results the existing branch has changed. CAL-212 remain as entry points for supplying this missing call evidence; until these questions are answered, a shared schema should not be presented as evidence of object ownership.
